Agelasticus xanthophthalmus: locally in marshes of eastern Ecuador and eastern Peru
Aglaeactis aliciae: east slope of Andes of northern Peru (La Libertad and Ancash)
Aglaeactis castelnaudii: humid montane, elfin and Polylepis forest in the Andes of south-central Peru, in Huánuco, Pasco and Junín and south in Ayacucho, Cusco and Apurimac
Aglaeactis cupripennis: treeline and shrubby paramo in the Andes from northeastern Colombia southward in the western and central Andes of Colombia across Ecuador to southeastern Peru, to Puno
Aglaeactis pamela: Andes of western Bolivia (La Paz and Cochabamba)
Aglaiocercus berlepschi: mountains of northeastern Venezuela (Sucre and Monagas)
Aglaiocercus coelestis: montane cloudforest in the western Andes from northern Colombia, in Antioquia, southward to southern Ecuador, in El Oro
Aglaiocercus kingii: montane cloudforest in the coastal mountains of northern Venezuela (Falcón eastward to Miranda), the Sierra de Perijá, and Andes of western Venezuela southward in the western, central, and eastern Andes of Colombia to the Andes of northwestern Ecuador, and in the eastern Andes of Ecuador southward to northern Peru north of the Río Marañón (Cajamarca), the eastern Andes from northern Peru south and east of the Marañón, southward to central Bolivia (western Santa Cruz)
Agraphospiza rubescens: coniferous forest of Nepal to southeastern Tibet and southwestern China
Agricola infuscatus: lowland acacia savanna, Karoo and Kalahari shrubland, and dry open woodland, from southwestern Angola and northern Botswana southward to western South Africa (eastward to Free State and Eastern Cape)
Agricola pallidus: lowland and foothill wooded savanna, miombo and mopane woodland, farmbush, and open secondary habitats, from Senegambia eastward to Eritrea, Ethiopia, and northern Somali, and southward to western Angola, northeastern Namibia, Botswana, Mozambique, and eastern South Africa; some local movement with rains
Agriornis albicauda: rare in dry paramo and puna with scattered trees, xeric scrub and rocky slopes in the Andes from northern Ecuador southward locally to northeastern Chile and very locally in northwestern Argentina (mainly Tucumán)
Agriornis lividus: dry to humid shrubland and agricultural fields from the coast of northern Chile southward to Patagonia in southern Chile and southern Argentina, mostly in the Andes (from Mendoza southward to northern Santa Cruz)
Agriornis micropterus: open shrubby steppe and shrubby puna grassland, resident in the Andes of southeastern Peru southward across Bolivia and adjacent northeastern Chile to northwestern Argentina, and breeds disjunctly in the sierras of Cordoba and in central Argentina (Mendoza southward to northern Tierra del Fuego); southern population winters in northern Argentina, western Uruguay, southernmost Brazil, western Paraguay, and likely southern Bolivia
Agriornis montanus: dry to semi-humid grassy paramo, puna, dry scrub, rocky fields, and agricultural land in the Andes from far southern Colombia southward to southern Chile and southern Argentina, northern coastal Chile (Iquique to Coquimbo), sierras of Córdoba and San Luis (north-central Argentina), very locally in southern Buenos Aires, and in south-central Argentina from Río Negro to Santa Cruz; southernmost populations winter to northward
Agriornis murinus: southern Argentina; winters northward to western Paraguay and southern Bolivia
Agropsar philippensis: breeds southern Sakhalin, Kuril Islands, and northern Japan; winters to Philippines, Sulawesi, and Borneo
Agropsar sturninus: breeds southeastern Siberia to northern Mongolia and northern Korea; winters to southeastern Asia
Ailuroedus buccoides: northwestern New Guinea eastward to southeastern Cenderawasih Bay, including Raja Ampat Islands (off western New Guinea)
Ailuroedus crassirostris: eastern Australia (Kroombit Tops, southeastern Queensland to southern New South Wales)
Ailuroedus geislerorum: northern lowlands and northern watershed of southeastern New Guinea, including Yapen (Cenderawasih Bay, off northwestern New Guinea)
Ailuroedus maculosus: northeastern Australia (Wet Tropics region, northern Queensland)
Ailuroedus melanotis: New Guinea, including Misool and Aru Islands), and northeastern Australia
Ailuroedus stonii: southern watershed of southern and southeastern New Guinea
Aimophila notosticta: arid highlands of southern Mexico (central Oaxaca)
Aimophila rufescens: Pacific slope from northern Sonora southward to Nayarit and central Tamaulipas on Caribbean slope, thence across transvolcanic belt and through Mexico (except Yucatan Peninsula) to southern Belize and eastern Nicaragua to northwestern Costa Rica
Aimophila ruficeps: north-central California disjunctly eastward to central Texas and southward through Mexico to southern Oaxaca (southeastern Mexico)
Aix galericulata: breeds wooded ponds, swamps, and streams of northeastern Asia from southeastern Siberia, eastern China, Korean Peninsula, Japan (Hokkaido to central Ryukyu Islands), and Taiwan; winters to southeastern China and northern southeastern Asia; introduced in Western Europe, and escapes frequent in USA
Aix sponsa: breeds mainly inland waters of southern Canada from southern British Colombia and Montana to southern California in the west, and eastern Saskatchewan eastward to Nova Scotia and southward to east-central Texas and southern Florida and Cuba; mainly resident in west of range; in east winters mainly from east-central USA southward to central Mexico and the Bahamas
Akletos goeldii: southeastern Peru to far northwestern Bolivia and far southwestern Amazonian Brazil
Akletos melanoceps: southeastern Colombia to northeastern Peru and western Amazonian Brazil
Alaemon alaudipes: semi-desert and desert with sparse vegetation, sandy or gravel soil in the Sahara from Cape Verde, Morocco, Western Sahara, and Mauritania eastward to the Red Sea coast, southward to northern Somalia, and in the Middle East, including southeasternmost Türkiye and Sinai Peninsula southward across the Arabian Peninsula to Yemen and Oman, and eastward across Iraq and Iran to southern Afghanistan, southern Pakistan, and westernmost India
Alauda arvensis: lowland to montane grassland, farmland, heath, steppe, and meadows, from British Isles and Scandinavia eastward to eastern Siberia and Kamchatka, and southward to northwestern Africa, southern Europe, northern Iran, and Japan; has bred Pribilof Islands, Alaska. Northern populations migrate southward to northern Africa, Middle East, northern India, and eastern China; introduced in Australia, New Zealand, Hawaiian Islands (all main islands), and Vancouver Island, British Columbia
Alauda gulgula: breeds southern and eastern Kazakhstan and eastern Turkmenistan eastward along the Himalayas and much of the Tibetan Plateau to eastern China, southward in southeastern Asia, Taiwan, and Philippines; winters to southeastern Arabian Peninsula, southwestern Asia, northern Bangladesh, northeastern India, and northern Myanmar
Alauda leucoptera: foothill and submontane arid steppe grassland, scrubby Artemisia steppe, and cultivation, from southwestern Russia and northern Kazakhstan eastward to northwestern China; winters to eastern Ukraine, northern Iran, and Kyrgyzstan
Alaudala cheleensis: Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, southern Kazakhstan, northern Mongolia, and adjacent parts of southern Siberia, and northern China
Alaudala heinei: sandy steppe and semi-desert from northern Kazakhstan and southernmost Russia southward to central Türkiye, southeastern Iraq, eastern Saudi Arabia, southern Iran, southern Afghanistan, and adjacent Pakistan, and southern Mongolia
Alaudala raytal: lowland to montane dry sandy riverbanks and islands of large rivers, sandy lakeshore, coastal semi-desert, and salt pans, from coastal eastern Iran eastward through northern India, Himalayan Nepal, and Bhutan, to western Myanmar
Alaudala rufescens: open areas with scattered low bushes in the Iberian Peninsula, the Canary Islands, and Morocco eastward across northern Algeria, Tunisia, Libya, and Egypt to southern Türkiye, Syria, and western Iraq, and southward in the Arabian Peninsula to southern Oman
Alaudala somalica: disjunctly in foothill and montane dry open grassland of eastern Ethiopia and northern Somalia, southern Ethiopia and adjacent northern Kenya, and southern Kenya and adjacent northern Tanzania
Alca torda: breeds rocky cliffs of low Arctic to north temperate North Atlantic coasts, from Greenland, Iceland, and British Isles to Scandinavia, northwestern France, and the White Sea (northwestern Russia), northeastern Canada to Nova Scotia and Gulf of Maine; winters south to Gulf Stream off North Carolina (western North Atlantic), and inland on St. Lawrence River; to Iberian Peninsula (eastern North Atlantic) and western Mediterranean Sea
Alcedo atthis: lowland to foothill lakes, ponds, small rivers, canals, and mangroves, from southern Sweden, British Isles, and northwestern Africa eastward to southern Siberia, Sakhalin, and Japan (Hokkaido to Ryukyu Islands), and southward to northern Iran, India, Sri Lanka, and southeastern Asia, and disjunctly from Sulawesi and Bali eastward through coastal New Guinea to the Bismarck and Solomon Archipelago; northern population migrate southward as far as Nile Valley (Egypt), Arabian Peninsula, Philippines, and Greater Sundas
Alcedo coerulescens: southern Sumatra, Java, Bali, Lombok, Sumbawa, and Kangean Islands
Alcedo hercules: Sikkim to southwestern China, Myanmar, northern Laos, northern Vietnam, and Hainan
Alcedo meninting: streams and creeks in humid to deciduous forest, mangroves, and bamboo forest in Western Ghats of Peninsular India from Maharashtra southward, northern Sri Lanka (very rare or vagrant), northern Eastern Ghats, and southern Nepal eastward to northeastern India and Bangladesh, thence southward through the Andaman Islands, southeastern Asia to southern Cambodia and Vietnam, the Malayan Peninsula to Singapore and satellite islands, Sumatra (including satellite islands), Bangka, Java eastward to Lombok, Borneo, Sulawesi region (Indonesia), and Palawan (southwestern Philippines)
Alcedo peninsulae: southern Myanmar, Malayan Peninsula, Sumatra, and Borneo
Alcedo quadribrachys: lowland to foothill papyrus swamps, rivers and lakes, ponds in forest, and tidal estuaries and mangroves, from Senegambia eastward to southern South Sudan and far western Kenya, and southward to northern Angola and northwestern Zambia
Alcedo semitorquata: Ethiopia, Angola to Tanzania, southern to Mozambique and southern South Africa
Alcippe brunneicauda: southern Thailand, Malayan Peninsula, Sumatra, Borneo, and North Natuna and Batu islands
Alcippe davidi: foothill to submontane broadleaf evergreen forest, secondary forest, scrub, and bamboo, in central China and northernmost Vietnam
Alcippe fratercula: foothill to submontane broadleaf evergreen forest, open secondary woodland, scrub, and bamboo, from northern Myanmar and south-central China southward to northwestern Thailand and central Vietnam
Alcippe grotei: southeastern Thailand and northern and central Annam and adjacent Laos
Alcippe hueti: hill forest of southeastern China (Guangdong to Anhui, and Hainan)
Alcippe nipalensis: foothill to submontane broadleaf evergreen and deciduous forest, secondary growth, and bamboo, from northern India eastward to northern Myanmar and adjacent China, and southward to northeastern India and western Myanmar
Alcippe peracensis: disjunctly in foothill to submontane broadleaf evergreen forest in southern Laos, adjacent northeastern Cambodia, and central Vietnam, and in peninsular Malayasia and adjacent southernmost Thailand
Alcippe poioicephala: foothill to submontane bushy understory in broadleaf forest, secondary growth, and bamboo scrub, from Peninsular India eastward to south-central China, and southward to southern Thailand and central Vietnam
Alcippe pyrrhoptera: forest of western and central Java
Alcurus striatus: foothill and submontane broadleaf forest, and oak-rhododendron woodland, from central Nepal eastward through Himalayas to south-central China, and southward to central Myanmar, northern Thailand, and northern Laos
Alectoris barbara: open dry rocky lowland to mountains from northern Western Sahara to Libya; also Sardinia (introduced?) and introduced Gibraltar and Canary Islands
Alectoris chukar: open dry often rocky areas of lowlands to high mountains from eastern Greece and southeastern Bulgaria to far southwestern Russia and Türkiye southward through Sinai (eastern Egypt) and northwestern Saudi Arabia, eastward through Iran, and northward through Turkmenistan, Kazakhstan, and Mongolia eastward to Liaoning (northeastern China); in south through Afghanistan, Pakistan, and western Himalayas through eastern Nepal; introduced to United Arab Emirates, South Island (New Zealand), Hawaiian Islands (all main islands), and southwestern Canada and western USA
Alectoris graeca: rocky slopes to open woodland of hill and montane central and southeastern Europe, from far southeastern France, Switzerland, and southwestern Austria through Italy, Sicily, Balkans, and Greece eastward to east-central Bulgaria
Alectoris magna: arid montane northern Qinghai and west-central Gansu (north-central China)
Alectoris melanocephala: arid regions of southern Arabian Peninsula to Yemen and Oman
Alectoris philbyi: rocky desert of southwestern Saudi Arabia and northern Yemen
Alectoris rufa: varied drier open habitats in lowlands to hills from Iberian Peninsula and France through northern Italy and Corsica; introduced to British Isles and from Azores southeast through Canary Islands
Alectrurus risora: locally in eastern Paraguay, southern Brazil, Uruguay, and northern Argentina
Alectrurus tricolor: locally in eastern Bolivia, northeastern Argentina, northeastern Paraguay, and southern Brazil
Alectura lathami: northern Cape York Peninsula to east-central New South Wales (eastern Australia)
Alethe castanea: lowland and foothill undergrowth in primary and old secondary forest, and forest patches in savanna, from southern Nigeria, and Bioko (Gulf of Guinea), eastward to southwestern South Sudan, and western Uganda, and southward to northern Angola, central and eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, and northwestern Tanzania
Alethe diademata: patchy in lowland primary and old secondary forest, gallery forest, forest patches in savanna, and plantations, from southwestern Senegal eastward to western Togo
Alipiopsitta xanthops: interior Brazil (Maranhão) to northern Paraguay and eastern Bolivia
Alisterus amboinensis: islands east of Sulawesi, Moluccas, and northwestern New Guinea
Alle alle: breeds scree slopes of coasts of high Arctic from northeastern Canada and Greenland to Franz Josef Land and Severnaya Zemlya, north-central Russia; more rarely to Bering Strait; winters south in Gulf Stream to North Carolina, and inland on St. Lawrence River; to northern British Isles and North Sea
Allenia fusca: varied wooded habitats in lowlands of Lesser Antilles from Saint-Martin/Sint Maarten and Saba through St. Vincent; likely extinct Barbados
Alophoixus flaveolus: foothill understory of evergreen forest from Nepal eastward to south-central China, and southward to Myanmar and western Thailand; some downslope dispersal in winter
Alophoixus frater: southwestern Philippines (Balabac, Busuanga, Calamianes, and Palawan)
Alophoixus ochraceus: humid forest in southern Myanmar (Tenasserim), southern Thailand, southern Cambodia, and southern Vietnam, southward through the Malayan Peninsula to Singapore and satellite islands, and western Sumatra
Alophoixus pallidus: lowland and foothill wooded habitat, from forest to riparian woodland, from central Myanmar and southern China (including Hainan), and southward through Indochina to southern Myanmar and southern Vietnam
Alophoixus phaeocephalus: Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, Mentawai Islands (west of central Sumatra), Bintang, Riau, and Lingga islands (east of central Sumatra), Bangka and Belitung (east of southern Sumatra), Natuna Islands (northwest of Borneo), and Borneo
Alophoixus tephrogenys: humid to mixed deciduous forest, tidal swamps, and adjacent open areas in lowlands and hills from far southern Myanmar (Tenasserim) and Peninsular Thailand southward to the southern Malayan peninsula, Sumatra, and Borneo
Alopochelidon fucata: Venezuela and northern Brazil; Brazil south of the Amazon River to northern Argentina
Alopochen aegyptiaca: Nile Valley of Egypt and Sudan, and sub-Saharan Africa; introduced to western and central Europe, and southeastern USA
Alopochen kervazoi: formerly Réunion; extinct, likely since late 1600s
Alopochen mauritiana: formerly Mauritius; extinct, likely since late 1600s
Amadina erythrocephala: western Angola eastward to southern Zambia and southwestern Zimbabwe, and southward to southern South Africa
Amadina fasciata: lowland and foothill grassy and mopane woodland, and acacia or palm savanna, across the Sahel from southern Mauritania and Senegambia eastward to southern Sudan, Eritrea, Ethiopia, and Somalia, southward through east Africa to southern Angola, and thence southward to southeastern Botswana and northeastern South Africa; nomadic and irruptive at times
Amalocichla sclateriana: montane central and southeastern New Guinea
Amandava amandava: lowland to submontane grassland, marsh, damp grass, reeds, rice fields, tamarisk scrub, and villages, from Pakistan eastward to south-central China (including Hainan), and southward to Peninsular India, Thailand, and southern Vietnam, and from Java eastward through Lesser Sundas to Timor; introduced widely, including Iberia, north-central Italy, the Nile Valley (Egypt), central and eastern Arabian Peninsula, Malaysia, Singapore, Fiji (majin islands), Hawaii (most main islands), and Guadeloupe and Martinique (Lesser Antilles)
Amandava formosa: locally in grassland and scrub of Peninsular India
Amandava subflava: widespread but patchy in sub-Saharan Africa (except rainforest and southwestern Africa), in lowland to montane grassland, open woodland, and marshes from southern Mauritania and Senegal eastward to western Ethiopia, southward to Angola and northern Botswana, and from eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda southward to eastern South Africa, nomadic during rains; also western Yemen (where possibly introduced?)
Amaurolimnas concolor: southern Mexico to Ecuador, the Guianas, Brazil, eastern Peru, and Bolivia
Amaurornis moluccana: Sangihe (north of Sulawesi), Sula Islands (east of Sulawesi), and Moluccas to New Guinea and satellite islands, Australia, and Solomon Archipelago
Amaurornis phoenicurus: Pakistan eastward in sub-Himalayan region to northeastern China, and southward to Maldives and Chagos (central Indian Ocean), southern India, Sri Lanka, Andaman and Nicobar islands, southeastern Asia, southern Japan (Ryukyu Islands), Indonesian Archipelago, Philippines, and Cocos (Keeling) and Christmas islands (east-central Indian Ocean)
Amaurospiza aequatorialis: mountains of southwestern Colombia (Nariño) to northern Peru (Cajamarca)
Amaurospiza carrizalensis: northern Venezuela (lower Río Caroni in Bolívar)
Amaurospiza concolor: montane bamboo thickets and humid forest on Pacific slope from southern Jalisco (west-central Mexico) discontinuously through Mexico and to Caribbean slope in Belize, southward to western Panama; nomadic
Amaurospiza moesta: locally from southeastern Paraguay to eastern Brazil and northeastern Argentina (Misiones)
Amazilia luciae: arid interior valleys of northern and central Honduras
Amazilia rutila: drier woodland of lowlands to hills on Pacific slope from northern Sinaloa southward to west-central Costa Rica, and on Caribbean slope on the Yucatan Peninsula (including Cozumel) and southward to southeastern Nicaragua
Amazilia tzacatl: humid to dry forest and scrub from eastern Mexico (from southern Veracruz, including interior Yucatan Peninsula) southward along the Gulf of Mexico slope to eastern Panama, and the Pacific slope from far eastern Nicaragua to Panama, the lowlands of northern Colombia and western Venezuela (except the Guajira Peninsula), southward to the headwaters of the Cauca and Magdalena valleys, west of the Andes southward along Pacific Colombia to southwestern Ecuador and adjacent Peru
Amazilia yucatanensis: scrub, edge, and gardens of lowlands to hills on Caribbean slope from southern Texas to Yucatan Peninsula (except Cozumel) southward to central Belize
Amazilis amazilia: arid forest and scrub in the lowlands of western Ecuador southward in western Peru (to Ica); also in the dry Andean valleys of southern Ecuador, and northern and southern Peru
Amazona aestiva: drier woodland with large trees from western Bolivia eastward to eastern Maranhão, southward to Córdoba (north-central Argentina) and eastward to Mato Grosso and western Paraná; introduced San Juan (eastern Puerto Rico), eastern seaboard of southern Brazil southward to Porto Alegre (Rio Grande do Sul, southeastern Brazil) and Buenos Aires (Argentina)
Amazona albifrons: semiarid woodland in lowlands and hills, from southern Sonora south on Pacific coast of Mexico, and from central Veracruz through Yucatan Peninsula and northwestern Central America to northwestern Costa Rica; introduced Los Angeles and San Diego (southern California), far southeastern Texas, Monterrey (Nuevo León, northeastern Mexico), Mexico City (Distrito Federal), and elsewhere
Amazona amazonica: humid forest in the lowlands of northern Colombia, southward along the Magdalena Valley to Cundinamarca and along the Cauca Valley to Valle del Cauca; in the lowlands of western and northern Venezuela, including Isla Margarita, eastward to Trinidad and Tobago and the Guianas; east of the Andes from the lowlands of central Venezuela southward across the western Amazon of eastern Colombia to northeastern Peru, and eastward across the entire Amazon of Brazil, eastward to northern Piauí and southward to southern Mato Grosso do Sul, adjacent Paraguay, and northern Bolivia; also in the Atlantic Forest of eastern Brazil from Rio Grande do Norte southward to Paraná
Amazona auropalliata: deciduous and other dry woodland of lowlands from Oaxaca (southeastern Mexico) on the Pacific slope through northwestern Costa Rica, and coastal northeastern Honduras and Bay Islands (north of Honduras) to northeastern Nicaragua
Amazona autumnalis: deciduous to humid forest from the Gulf of Mexico slope in southern Tamaulipas southeastward across the Caribbean lowlands of Central America to Panama, and in the Pacific lowlands of Costa Rica and adjacent Nicaragua, eastward to Panama (including Coiba); in South America in the lowlands of northern Colombia and western Venezuela, southward along the Magdalena Valley (to Valle del Cauca); west of the Andes along the Pacific lowlands of Colombia
Amazona barbadensis: coastal northern Venezuela including islas Margarita and La Blanquilla; Bonaire
Amazona brasiliensis: southeastern Brazil (southeastern São Paulo and Paraná)
Amazona diadema: northwestern Brazil (lower Rio Negro and north bank of the upper Amazon River)
Amazona dufresniana: southeastern Venezuela (Gran Sabana) to the Guianas and (?) adjacent Brazil
Amazona farinosa: deciduous and gallery to humid forest from the Gulf of Mexico slope in eastern Mexico, from southern Veracruz and northern Oaxaca southeastward across the Caribbean side of Central America to Panama, also in the Pacific lowlands of Costa Rica to Panama, including the Azuero Peninsula and Coiba; in the lowlands of northern South America in Colombia and western Venezuela, south along the Magdalena Valley to Tolima, and west of the Andes southward to west-central Ecuador; east of the Andes in the Orinoco basin from eastern and central Venezuela eastward across the Guianas and southward across the Amazon of southern Venezuela, eastern Colombia, eastern Ecuador, eastern Peru, northern and central Bolivia, and Brazil eastward to northern Maranhão and southward to central Mato Grosso; also in the Atlantic Forest of eastern Brazil (southern Bahia southward to São Paulo)
Amazona festiva: tropical rainforest of the Orinoco basin from eastern Venezuela and adjacent Guyana southwestward to northeastern Colombia; in the Amazon basin from southeastern Colombia and northeastern Ecuador southward to northeastern Peru, southward to northern Ucayali, and eastward along the Amazon River of northern Brazil to the mouth of the Amazon River and north to Roraima
Amazona finschi: western Mexico (southern Sonora, Chihuahua, and Durango to Oaxaca)
Amazona guildingii: montane forest of St. Vincent (Lesser Antilles)
Amazona leucocephala: drier woodland and gardens of Abaco and Great Inagua (north and south Bahamas), Cuba including Isla de la Juventud (Isle of Pines), and Grand Cayman and Cayman Brac (western and eastern Cayman islands)
Amazona lilacina: southwestern Ecuador (north shore of the Bahia de Caráque in central Manabí southward to Gulf of Guayaquil and El Oro); possibly farther north in western Ecuador
Amazona mercenarius: montane cloudforest in Sierra de Perijá, Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, the Andes from western Venezuela southward along the western, central, and eastern Andes of Colombia, in western Ecuador (to northern El Oro), and in the eastern Andes southward across Ecuador and Peru to central Bolivia (western Santa Cruz)
Amazona ochrocephala: humid forest from western Panama to the lowlands of northern Colombia and western Venezuela, southward along the Cauca and Magdalena valleys (to Valle del Cauca and Tolima); east of the Andes from the lowlands of northern Venezuela, Trinidad and the Guianas south and westward across the Amazon basin of southern Venezuela, eastern Colombia, Ecuador and Peru, to northern Bolivia, and Brazil eastward to northern Maranhão, Isla de Marajó and southward to southern Mato Grosso
Amazona oratrix: deciduous and other dry woodland types in lowlands to hills on Caribbean slope from Tamaulipas through southern Yucatan Peninsula to northwestern Honduras, and Pacific slope from Nayarit to southern Oaxaca; Tres Marias Islands
Amazona pretrei: Araucaria and broadleaf forest of southeastern Brazil (Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul)
Amazona rhodocorytha: eastern Brazil (Alagoas and Bahia to Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo)
Amazona tucumana: montane forest of southeastern Bolivia and northwestern Argentina
Amazona versicolor: montane forest of St. Lucia (Lesser Antilles)
Amazona vinacea: Araucaria and broadleaf forest of eastern Brazil (Bahia) to eastern Paraguay and northern Argentina (rare)
Amazona viridigenalis: lowlands of northeastern Mexico (Nuevo León to northern Veracruz)
Amazona vittata: formerly widespread in Puerto Rico; a small wild population survives in forest of El Yunque (northeastern Puerto Rico), with reintroductions in Maricao and Río Abajo (western Puerto Rico)
Amazona xantholora: southeastern Mexico (Yucatan Peninsula and Cozumel) to Belize
Amazonetta brasiliensis: smaller lowland wetlands, mostly in wooded areas, of cis-Andean South America from east-central Colombia east throughout Brazil and southward to northwestern and east-central Argentina
Amblycercus holosericeus: disjunctly in dry to humid montane forest and bamboo from the Gulf slope in southern Tamaulipas and on the Pacific slope from Chiapas (southeastern Mexico) southward through Central America, including the Yucatan Peninsula, to Panama and northwestern Colombia, west of the Andes southward to northwestern Peru, in Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, Sierra de Perijá, and the coastal mountains of northern Venezuela, and the Andes from western Venezuela southward to northern Peru north of the Río Marañón, and the eastern Andes from northern Peru southward to central Bolivia (Cochabamba)
Amblyornis inornata: northwestern New Guinea (Arfak, Tamrau, and Wandammen mountains)
Amblyornis subalaris: southeastern Papua New Guinea (Owen Stanley Mountains)
Amblyospiza albifrons: patchy in lowland to montane woodland near wetlands from Sierra Leone eastward to southwestern Central African Republic, and southward to western Angola and southern Democratic Republic of the Congo, and from Ethiopia and southern Somalia southward through Tanzania, including Pemba and Unguja (in Zanzibar), to Zambia and Mozambique, and westward to northeastern Namibia, thence southward to eastern South Africa
Amblyramphus holosericeus: marshes of northern Bolivia (Beni and Santa Cruz), Paraguay, southern Brazil, and northern Argentina
Amirafra angolensis: montane and recently burned grassland, from western Angola eastward to northwestern Zambia and southwestern Tanzania
Amirafra collaris: patchy in lowland to foothill semiarid savanna, grassland with scattered shrubs on red sands, and open acacia woodland, from eastern Ethiopia and northern and central Somalia, and southward to eastern Kenya
Amirafra rufocinnamomea: lowland and foothill savanna, open woodland, and grassy dambos in closed woodland, from Senegambia eastward to Ethiopia and southern Somalia, and southward (avoiding rainforest) to northeastern Namibia and northeastern South Africa
Ammodramus aurifrons: varied open habitats including highly disturbed areas, from short grass, riparian grass, and river islands in the Orinoco basin from northeastern Venezuela and the llanos of southwestern Venezuela and northeastern Colombia southward to central Bolivia, Amazonian Brazil (mostly along large rivers, eastward to western Maranhão, southward to Rondônia, and western Mato Grosso), and in the Cerrado of interior Brazil (southward to western Goiás)
Ammodramus humeralis: grasslands, savanna, and agricultural fields in northern and central Colombia eastward through the Guianas southward to northern Brazil (Roraima, Amapá, and northern Pará), and in Cerrado, Caatinga and Atlantic Forest region from northeastern Brazil southward to central Argentina (southern Buenos Aires) and westward to southeastern Peru; spreading to eastern and central Amazon basin
Ammodramus savannarum: breeds short-grass prairies, grasslands, and shrubby savanna from southern British Columbia eastward to southern Quebec and southward in western USA to southern California, and from western Texas eastward to central Florida, and very locally in interior western USA, southern Mexico through central Panama, Jamaica, Hispaniola, and Puerto Rico, and Curaçao and Bonaire, and in dry montane valleys in central to southern Colombia and (formerly) northern Ecuador; northern populations winter in southern USA southward to southern Honduras and El Salvador, and Cuba
Ammomanes cinctura: semi-desert and desert with very sparse vegetation in flat or undulating terrain in Cabo Verde and the Sahara from Morocco, Western Sahara, and Mauritania eastward to the Red Sea coast of eastern Egypt and Sudan, in the Sinai Peninsula, southern Israel, and southern Syria southward to Yemen and Oman, and eastward to southern Afghanistan and southern Pakistan
Ammomanes deserti: rocky and stony hills in desert and semi-desert from northwestern Africa (Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia) eastward to the Red Sea coast of northeastern Africa and southward to southern Ethiopia and Somalia; in the Middle East and Arabian Peninsula eastward across Iraq and Iran to Pakistan and westernmost India, including western Uzbekistan and adjacent southern Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, and southwestern Tajikistan
Ammomanes phoenicura: open scrub forest, savanna, deciduous forest and woodland, fallow fields, and dry rocky grasslands in the Jhelum River basin in northern Pakistan and from northwestern India, in southern Punjab, and northeastern India, south of the Ganges River, southward to southern Peninsular India
Ammomanopsis grayi: lowland gravel plain, and saltflats with sparse vegetation, of southwestern Angola and coastal Namibia
Ammonastes pelzelni: far eastern Colombia to southwestern Venezuela and far northwestern Brazil
Ammoperdix griseogularis: dry foothills and plateaus of southeastern Türkiye, northern Syria, and (locally) northern Saudi Arabia to southern Armenia, Uzbekistan, southeastern Turkmenistan, southern Tajikistan southward through Iran and Afghanistan (except northeastern), to sub-Himalayan Pakistan

Anthus campestris: breeds central and southern Europe and northwestern Africa (Morocco eastward to Tunisia) eastward to northwestern and south-central Mongolia, northwestern Kazakhstan, northern Afghanistan, and far northwestern China, also locally in Middle East; winters in sub-Saharan Africa (mainly in the Sahel), Arabian Peninsula, and southwestern Asia
Anthus cervinus: breeds tundra of northern Palearctic and northwestern Alaska; winters to Africa, Indonesia, and Philippines
Anthus chacoensis: locally in Chaco of eastern Paraguay and northern Argentina
Anthus chii: disjunctly in varied grasslands including open fields with short grass, in western and central Panama, from the llanos of central Colombia eastward to the Guianas, almost throughout Brazil (except western Amazonas and western Acre) westward to far southeastern Peru (Madre de Dios), and southward to east-central Argentina (La Pampa)
Anthus cinnamomeus: widespread sub-Saharan Africa in lowland to montane grassland, savanna, and farmland (but absent from west Africa and Congolian rainforest), from southeastern Nigeria eastward through southern Sudan, Eritrea, and Ethiopia, to northern Somalia, plus southwestern Arabian Peninsula, and southward to southern Africa; southern populations migrate northward in non-breeding season, also some downslope movement
Anthus correndera: dry puna grassland, bogs and wetland edges, and Patagonian steppe from the Andes of central Peru (Ancash), locally in southeastern Paraguay, and southeastern Brazil (Santa Catarina), southward to far southern Chile and Argentina and the Falkland Islands
Anthus crenatus: foothill to montane steep rocky scree slopes, alpine grassland with boulders or shrub, and grassy Karoo, in South Africa and Lesotho
Anthus furcatus: far southeastern Brazil to Paraguay, Uruguay, and northern Argentina
Anthus godlewskii: southern Siberia to Mongolia, China, Tibet, and northeastern India
Anthus gustavi: lowland tundra scrub and swampy taiga from northern Russia eastward to eastern Siberia, Kamchatka, and Commander Islands, and southward to northeastern China and adjacent Ussuriland; migrates to Philippines, Borneo, and Wallacea
Anthus hellmayri: disjunctly in varied open grassland habitats from paramo and puna to rocky fields in the Andes of southeastern Peru (Ayacucho and Puno) southward to south-central Chile and southern Argentina (Santa Cruz; breeding only), sierras of Cordoba and San Luis (north-central Argentina), and southeastern Brazil from central Minas Gerais southward to eastern Paraguay and east-central Argentina (Rio Negro); southern populations winter to northern Argentina
Anthus hodgsoni: lowland to montane taiga edge, rocky ground in open forest, scrub above treeline, and scrub with isolated trees, from northwestern Russia eastward to Kamchatka and northern Japan (Hokkaido), and southward through central China to Himalayas from Kashmir eastward to south-central China; migrates to southern India, southeastern China (including Hainan), and Taiwan, and to southeastern Asia, Borneo, and Philippines
Anthus hoeschi: submontane to montane short grassland in Drakensberg of eastern South Africa and Lesotho; migrates to eastern Angola, southern Democratic Republic of the Congo, and northwestern Zambia
Anthus japonicus: breeds northern to eastern Russia in southeastern Taymyr Peninsula, western Siberian Plateau, and from eastward of Lena River, Yakutsk region, and Lake Baikal eastward to Chukotskiy Peninsula, Commander Islands, Sakhalin, and Kuril Islands; winters from central Japan and Korean Peninsula to southern and southeastern continental Asia
Anthus leucophrys: widespread sub-Saharan Africa in lowland and foothill lightly-wooded savanna, brushy grassland, and floodplains from southern Mauritania and Senegambia to southeastern Sudan, Eritrea, and Somalia southward to South Africa
Anthus lineiventris: Rwanda and southern Kenya southward to eastern South Africa; disjunctly western Angola
Anthus melindae: coastal lowland grassland and dunes from southern Somali to coastal southeastern Tanzania
Anthus nattereri: locally in southeastern Brazil, southeastern Paraguay, and northeastern Argentina
Anthus nicholsoni: lowland to montane arid veld, stony scrub, or rocky woodland from southwest Angola and western Namibia to southeastern Botswana and southern Zimbabwe (except Kalahari Desert), and southward to South Africa (eastward to Limpopo and KwaZulu-Natal), plus Lesotho and Eswatini
Anthus nilghiriensis: montane grassland of southwestern India (western Tamil Nadu and Kerala)
Anthus nyassae: lowland and foothill broadleaf woodland, wooded savanna, and miombo from southeastern Gabon and southern Republic of the Congo, eastward through southern Democratic Republic of the Congo to southern Tanzania, and southward to northern Namibia, northern Botswana, Malawi, Zimbabwe, and nearby Mozambique
Anthus pallidiventris: lowland grassland and forest clearings from southern Cameroon to northwest Angola and eastward through Gabon, southern Central African Republic, and Republic of the Congo to eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo; locally nomadic in non-breeding season
Anthus peruvianus: coastal northern Peru (Lambayeque) to far northern Chile (Tacna)
Anthus petrosus: lowland rocky coastal shore, and islands with low vegetation, from British Isles and Scandinavia eastward to northwestern Russia; migrates to coastal western Europe and northwestern Africa
Anthus pratensis: breeds Iceland and Faroe Islands through western and northern Europe eastward to western Russia; winters to northern Africa and central Asia
Anthus richardi: lowland to foothill grassland, open steppe, paddyfields, cultivation, and marsh edge, from southwestern Siberia and eastern Kazakhstan eastward to Ussuriland (Russia), and southward to northwestern and southeastern China; migrates to southern and southeastern Asia, and Taiwan
Anthus roseatus: breeds eastern Afghanistan to southeastern Tibet and southwestern China; winters to southeastern Asia
Anthus rubescens: breeds northern Alaska including Aleutians through northeastern Canada and western Greenland, and southward through mountains of western North America to Arizona and New Mexico; winters to south-central Mexico and Florida
Anthus rufulus: lowland to submontane open country, short grassland, paddyfields, cultivation, and wetland edge, from Afghanistan and Pakistan eastward to south-central China and northern Vietnam, and southward to Sri Lanka, Philippines, Greater Sundas, Sulawesi, and Lesser Sundas
Anthus similis: mountains of southwestern Mali, Guinea, and Sierra Leone to western Himalayas, southwestern India, and central Myanmar
Anthus sokokensis: local in lowland coastal forest and undisturbed miombo woodland in southeastern Kenya and northeastern Tanzania
Anthus spinoletta: patchy in lowland to montane alpine meadows, short grassland, and rocky scree with thickets, from mountains of central and southern Europe eastward to eastern Kazakhstan and Mongolia, and southward to Caucasus, northern Iran, and northwestern and central China; most migrate to western Europe, northwestern Africa, Middle East, Pakistan, and southern China
Anthus spragueii: breeds prairies and plains of North America; winters to southern Mexico
Anthus sylvanus: Himalayas (eastern Afghanistan to Nepal and southeastern China)
Anthus trivialis: lowland to montane open woodland, woodland edge, and grassland with scrub or scattered trees, from Britain and Scandinavia eastward to central Siberia, and southward to southern Europe, Caucasus, northern Pakistan through Kashmir; winters to sub-Saharan Africa and southern India
Anthus vaalensis: lowland grassland and overgrazed or burnt clearings from western Angola eastward through southern Democratic Republic of the Congo to southern Tanzania, southward through Zambia and Malawi to Namibia, Botswana, and eastern South Africa and adjacent Mozambique (but not southern Namibia and western South Africa); some post-breeding dispersal
Antigone antigone: patchy in lowland grassland, shallow marsh, natural wetland, and cultivated and fallow fields, from southern Pakistan and northwestern India south of the Himalayas eastward through southern Myanmar to southern Vietnam and in northeastern Australia; southeastern Asian populations winter to upper Mekong delta (Vietnam); extirpated from northern Philippines
Antigone canadensis: shallow marshes, bogs, sedge meadows and open grassland from eastern Siberia, northwestern Alaska and northern Canada, including Baffin Island, southward across most Canada to northern US (southward to northern California, western Montana southward to northwestern Colorado), and in the lower Mississippi basin, southeastern Georgia and northern Florida, and Cuba; winters in southern US and northern Mexico, with small numbers along eastern Chinese coast and southwestern Japan (Kyushu)
Antigone rubicunda: south-central New Guinea and northern and eastern Australia (Kimberley region, northern Northern Territory eastward to Queensland and southward to central New South Wales and western Victoria)
Antigone vipio: breeds northeastern Mongolia, northeastern China, and southeastern Russia; winters east-central China, Korean Peninsula, and southern Japan (western Kyushu)
Antiurus maculicaudus: locally from southeastern Mexico to northern Bolivia, eastern Paraguay, and southeastern Brazil
Antrostomus arizonae: breeds montane forest of southeastern California to southwestern Texas (southwestern USA) southward through Mexico including southern Baja California to southern Honduras; withdraws mostly south of USA in winter
Antrostomus badius: Yucatan Peninsula and Cozumel; winters to Belize and northern Honduras
Antrostomus carolinensis: breeds eastern USA; winters southeastern USA to Greater Antilles and northern South America
Antrostomus cubanensis: forest and scrub in lowlands and hills of Cuba and satellite islands
Antrostomus noctitherus: dry lowland forest of southwestern Puerto Rico
Antrostomus ridgwayi: rocky arid areas from lowlands to mountains of southeastern Arizona (southwestern USA) south on Pacific slope to western Nicaragua and northwestern Costa Rica (where rare)
Antrostomus rufus: dry to humid forest, woodland and scrub from southwestern Costa Rica eastward to northern Colombia, northern Venezuela, Trinidad, and St. Lucia (Lesser Antilles); in Venezuela also the Orinoco basin southwestward to the llanos of northeastern Colombia, eastward to northern Guianas, and southward to northern Brazil; widespread in Brazil in the Amazon basin, interior Brazil, and the Atlantic Forest, southward to northern and eastern Bolivia, Paraguay, and northwestern and northeastern Argentina, where seasonal; also locally in the foothills of the Andes of southeasternmost Ecuador and eastern Peru
Antrostomus salvini: tropical eastern Mexico (Nuevo León to Oaxaca and Chiapas)
Antrostomus saturatus: montane forest of Costa Rica and western Panama
Antrostomus sericocaudatus: tropical rainforest and scrubby forest borders in the Amazon basin in eastern Peru and far southeastern Colombia southward to northwestern Bolivia and eastward in Brazil, south of the Amazon River, to eastern Pará, adjacent Maranhão, and western Tocantins, and in northwestern Mato Grosso, Rondônia and adjacent northeastern Bolivia; also in the Atlantic Forest of southeastern Brazil from southern São Paulo southwestward to Santa Catarina, adjacent Rio Grande do Sul, far northeastern Argentina, and eastern Paraguay
Antrostomus vociferus: breeds southern Canada and eastern USA; winters to Cuba and western Panama
Anumara forbesi: northeastern and eastern Brazil, where very localized in Pernambuco and Alagoas, and northern Minas Gerais
Anumbius annumbi: savanna of Paraguay to southern Brazil, Uruguay, and central Argentina
Anurolimnas castaneiceps: damp thickets and dense second growth in the western Amazon basin from southeastern Colombia southward across eastern Ecuador and Peru to northwestern Bolivia and western Brazil, in southern Amazonas, Acre, and adjacent Rondônia
Apalis alticola: foothill and montane forest, and secondary growth, from northern and central Angola and southern Democratic Republic of the Congo eastward to northern Tanzania, and southward to northern Zambia and Malawi
Apalis argentea: patchy in submontane to montane primary forest, forest edge and bamboo thickets, dry forest, and secondary growth, from eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo eastward to Rwanda, Burundi, and western Tanzania
Apalis bamendae: patchy in foothill to submontane gallery forest in wooded savanna, thickets, and wooded orchards, in southeastern Nigeria, southwestern and central Cameroon, and possibly far western Central African Republic
Apalis binotata: disjunctly in foothill to submontane forest understory, old forest clearings, and secondary growth, in southern Cameroon and northern Gabon, and in northwestern Angola, and in northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, Uganda, and northern Tanzania
Apalis chapini: montane forest of central and southern Tanzania, northeastern Zambia, and Malawi
Apalis chariessa: disjunctly in foothill and montane forest of central and southern Tanzania, and of southern Malawi and adjacent Mozambique; apparently extinct in eastern Kenya
Apalis chirindensis: foothill and montane forest of eastern Zimbabwe highlands and central Mozambique
Apalis cinerea: disjunctly in foothill and montane forest and secondary growth of southeastern Nigeria, southwestern Cameroon, and Bioko (Gulf of Guinea), and from northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, southern South Sudan, and western Kenya southward to Burundi and northern Tanzania, and western Angola
Apalis flavida: lowland to montane mesic forest, acacia savanna, riparian thickets, and mangroves, from Senegambia eastward to Ethiopia and Somalia, and widespread southward (avoiding rainforest) to northern Namibia, northern Botswana, and southern South Africa
Apalis flavigularis: patchy in submontane to montane forest edge, riparian thickets, and secondary scrub, in highlands of southeastern Malawi, and possibly adjacent Mozambique
Apalis fuscigularis: foothill to submontane forest edge on mountaintops in southeastern Kenya (Taita Hills)
Apalis goslingi: disjunctly in lowland forest along rivers, forest edge, and secondary growth, from southern Cameroon and mainland Equatorial Guinea eastward to northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, and disjunctly northeastern Angola and adjacent Democratic Republic of the Congo
Apalis jacksoni: patchy in lowland to montane forest from southeastern Nigeria and southwestern Cameroon eastward to southern South Sudan and western Kenya, and southward to northwestern Angola, eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Burundi
Apalis kaboboensis: submontane and montane forest canopy in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (Mt. Kabobo)
Apalis karamojae: patchy in foothill savanna, acacia scrub along watercourses, and seasonally flooded plain, in northeastern Uganda (Kanatorok, in Kidepo Valley, and mts. Moroto, Kamalinga, and Kadam)
Apalis lynesi: submontane forest edge and canopy in northern Mozambique (Mt. Namuli)
Apalis melanocephala: lowland to montane forest, riverine woodland, and coastal scrub, from southern Somalia, central and eastern Kenya, and eastern Tanzania, and southward to Malawi, far eastern Zimbabwe, and Mozambique
Apalis nigriceps: lowland and foothill rainforest from Sierra Leone and southern Guinea eastward through southern Nigeria and Bioko (Gulf of Guinea) to Uganda, and southward to northern Gabon and eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo
Apalis personata: montane forest from northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo and southwestern Uganda southward to Burundi and southeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo
Apalis porphyrolaema: eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo eastward through southwestern Kenya and northern Tanzania
Apalis ruddi: lowland and foothill dry woodland, riverine scrub, and dense acacia thickets from southern Malawi southward through southern Mozambique to eastern South Africa
Apalis rufogularis: lowland to montane rainforest from southern Benin and southern Nigeria, and Bioko (Gulf of Guinea), eastward through Central African Republic and Democratic Republic of the Congo to western Kenya, thence southward to northwestern Angola, northwestern Zambia, and northwestern Tanzania
Apalis sharpii: lowland Upper Guinean rainforest canopy, dry deciduous forest, gallery forest, and mature secondary forest, from southern Guinea and Sierra Leone to western Togo
Apalis stronachi: patchy in foothill savanna, acacia scrub along watercourses, and seasonally flooded plain, in southwestern Kenya (Maasai Mara) and northern Tanzania (Serengeti)
Apalis thoracica: lowland to montane forest, riparian woodland, semiarid savanna, and coastal scrub, from southeastern Kenya southward through eastern Zambia and eastern Botswana to eastern and southern South Africa (westward to Western Cape)
Apaloderma aequatoriale: lowland rainforest of Cameroon, Gabon, and northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo
Apaloderma narina: lowland to montane rainforest, gallery forest, juniper woodland, dense scrub, and wooded savanna, of eastern Senegal and southwestern Mali, and from Sierra Leone eastward to Eritrea, Ethiopia, and western Somalia, and in the south from Angola and northeastern Namibia to southern South Africa; some populations undertake altitudinal migration
Apaloderma vittatum: southeastern Nigeria eastward to Kenya and southward to central Angola and Mozambique
Apalopteron familiare: Ogasawara (Bonin) Islands (southeastern Japan); Hahajima and satellites, and formerly Mukojima (where extinct)
Aphanotriccus audax: tropical eastern Panama and northern Colombia
Aphanotriccus capitalis: eastern Nicaragua to northern Costa Rica (southward to Puerto Limón)
Aphelocephala nigricincta: central Australia (Mount Magnet eastward to southwestern Queensland and northwestern New South Wales)
Aphelocephala pectoralis: south-central Australia (Marla southward to Lyndhurst, South Australia)
Aphelocoma californica: mostly shrubland, chaparral, and oak-pine woodland from far southwestern British Columbia (southwestern Canada) along Pacific coast and interior Washington and Oregon, southward to southern Baja California
Aphelocoma coerulescens: locally in central peninsular and Atlantic coastal Florida
Aphelocoma insularis: Santa Cruz Island (Channel Islands off southern California)
Aphelocoma ultramarina: montane pine and pine-oak from western Jalisco eastward to west-central Veracruz (central Mexico)
Aphelocoma unicolor: montane forest of Hidalgo to Veracruz and northern Oaxaca and on Pacific side in Guerrero, disjunctly in Chiapas to Honduras and far north-central Nicaragua
Aphelocoma wollweberi: oak and/or pine in mountains of south-central Arizona and southwestern New Mexico, and southwestern Texas southward to Jalisco in the west and Hidalgo in the east (central Mexico)
Aphelocoma woodhouseii: pinyon-juniper (mainly) and other scrub and woodland from northwestern Nevada, southern Idaho, and southern Wyoming southward through eastern California and central Texas through mountains of Mexico to Oaxaca
Aphrastura masafuerae: Alejandro Selkirk Island (Juan Fernández Islands off Chile)
Aphrastura spinicauda: humid temperate forest and scrub in central Chile, from southern region of Coquimbo, and far western Argentina in Mendoza, southward to Tierra del Fuego including Isla de los Estados, Isla Hornos and Diego Ramirez archipelago
Aphrodroma brevirostris: breeds South Georgia, Gough, Inaccessible, Prince Edward, Crozet, and Kerguelen islands; ranges subantarctic and Antarctic waters north of pack-ice
Aplonis brunneicapillus: Bougainville, Guadalcanal, Choiseul, and Rendova (northern Solomon Archipelago)
Aplonis cantoroides: New Guinea including Aru Islands, northwestern Torres Strait islands (northeastern Australia), Bismarck Archipelago, and Solomon Islands
Aplonis corvina: formerly Kosrae Island (Micronesia); extinct, last reported 1880
Aplonis feadensis: islets of Bismarck Archipelago and northern Solomon Islands
Aplonis fusca: formerly Lord Howe and Norfolk islands; extinct, last reported 1923
Aplonis mavornata: formerly Cook Islands; extinct, last reported 1825
Aplonis metallica: Moluccas, Tanimbar Islands, Damar Island, New Guinea including satellite islands, and northeastern Australia
Aplonis minor: Sulawesi, Java, Bali, Lesser Sundas, and southern Philippines (Mindanao)
Aplonis mysolensis: eastern Sulawesi, including Banggai and Sula Islands; Moluccas and west Papuan islands
Aplonis mystacea: lowland rainforest of southern New Guinea
Aplonis opaca: Mariana and Caroline island (western and central Micronesia)
Aplonis panayensis: Assam to Bangladesh and Myanmar (Arakan Mountains) southward through Thai-Malay Peninsula, Andaman and Nicobar islands, Sumatra, Java, Borneo, Philippines, and northern Sulawesi, including many satellite islands
Aplonis pelzelni: rediscovered 1995 in mountains of Pohnpei after 50-year absence but no recent records
Aplonis tabuensis: southeastern Melanesia in Temotu (=Santa Cruz, southeastern Solomon Islands) through southern Polynesia
Aplonis zelandica: Santa Cruz Islands (Temotu, southeastern Solomon Islands) and northern and central Vanuatu
Aplopelia larvata: patchy across sub-Saharan Africa in lowland and montane forest from Sierra Leone and Guinea to Cameroon and southward to northwestern Angola and on Gulf of Guinea islands, and from South Sudan and Ethiopia southward to Zambia and Malawi, and from eastern Zimbabwe and northern Mozambique to southern South Africa
Aprositornis disjuncta: locally in eastern Colombia, southwestern Venezuela, and northwestern Brazil (Amazonas)
Aprosmictus erythropterus: south-central New Guinea and northern and eastern Australia
Aprosmictus jonquillaceus: Rote, Timor, and Wetar (eastern Lesser Sundas)
Aptenodytes forsteri: breeds in scattered colonies on Antarctic continent edge and up to 200 km from open sea; ranges Antarctic seas to edge of ice pack and beyond, juveniles dispersing most widely
Aptenodytes patagonicus: breeds on beaches of subantarctic islands, in Tierra del Fuego, Falkland Islands, South Georgia, South Sandwich Islands, Prince Edward, Crozet, Kerguelen, and Heard islands, and Macquarie Island (southeast of Australia); disperses widely at sea mostly around Antarctic Convergence
Apteryx australis: southwestern South Island and Stewart Island (New Zealand)
Apteryx maxima: montane forest of northwestern South Island (New Zealand)
Apteryx owenii: Kapiti, South, and formerly North islands (New Zealand)
Apteryx rowi: Okarito Forest (west coast of South Island, New Zealand)
Apus acuticauda: breeds eastern Bhutan and northeastern India; winters to northern Thailand
Apus affinis: lowland to foothill woodland, cultivation, and towns and cities, Africa including Gulf of Guinea islands eastward to sub-Himalayan India, southward to southern India and Sri Lanka, eastward through the Himalayas to southern China (including Hainan) and Taiwan, and to South Korea and Japan, and southward through Greater Sundas and Philippines, to Sulawesi and Lesser Sundas; some northern populations move southward in winter
Apus apus: lowland to montane habitats, wide-ranging from woodland to semi-desert steppe, from western Europe eastward to central Siberia, and southward to northwestern Africa, Iran, northwestern India, and central China; long-distance migrant to central and southern Africa
Apus barbatus: foothill and montane cliffs from Sierra Leone eastward through Cameroon, and Bioko (Gulf of Guinea) to northern Kenya, and southward to Angola and South Africa; some populations are intra-African migrants
Apus batesi: humid forest of western Cameroon to northern Gabon and eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo
Apus berliozi: breeds in coastal cliffs and caves and arid and montane habitats in coastal Yemen (including Socotra) and Oman, and coastal Somalia; as non-breeder also in southern Kenya
Apus bradfieldi: lowland and foothill arid habitats, including desert, savanna, cliffs, and cities, from southwestern Angola southward through Namibia to northwestern South Africa
Apus caffer: southern Iberian Peninsula, central Morocco, and sub-Saharan Africa
Apus horus: Nigeria and Cameroon eastward to Ethiopia and southward to western Angola and southern South Africa
Apus niansae: disjunctly in lowland to montane cliffs and gorges in mostly arid highlands of Eritrea, Ethiopia, and northern Somalia, and northeastern Uganda, western Kenya, and northern Tanzania; Somali population migratory, mostly westward and southward
Apus pacificus: breeds Siberia to Kamchatka, northern China, Himalayas and Assam Hills, and Japan (Hokkaido to Kyushu), eastern China, Taiwan, northern Philippines (Batan Islands), lowland Myanmar, Thailand, Vietnam, southern Yunnan, and Guangxi (southwestern and southeastern China); winters India, southeastern Asia, Indonesia, Melanesia, and Australia (including Tasmania but not western deserts)
Apus pallidus: patchy in lowland to montane forest, sea-cliffs and gorges, and urban areas, from Iberia eastward to southern Iran, and southward to western Mauritania, locally in the Sahara, and Egypt and Arabian Peninsula; northern populations winter to the African Sahel, and coastal Pakistan
Apus unicolor: breeds Madeira and western Canary Islands; winters in northern Africa
Aquila adalberti: locally in Iberian Peninsula; formerly Morocco
Aquila africana: humid forest of western and central Africa
Aquila audax: south-central New Guinea, and Australia including Tasmania
Aquila chrysaetos: coastal deserts, highland shrub-steppe, coniferous forest, tundra, riparian woodland, and open areas from Scandinavia, northern British Isles, western Russia, and southern Europe southward to central Mauritania, northeastern Mali, northern Niger, the Arabian Peninsula and central Ethiopia, and eastward across Russia, Türkiye, the Caucasus, Iran, Kazakhstan, and Himalayas to eastern China, the Kamchatka Peninsula, the Korean Peninsula, Japan, and Alaska, northwestern and northeastern Canada southward across western US to northern Mexico
Aquila fasciata: patchy in lowland to submontane broken terrain with crags and cliffs, brushy slopes, and wooded grassland, from northwestern Africa and Iberia eastward through the Mediterranean, Middle East, and Arabian Peninsula, to India and southeastern China, and in the Lesser Sundas (Sumbawa to Timor and associated islands); some post-breeding dispersion southward to Senegal and Djibouti
Aquila gurneyi: Moluccas to New Guinea, including Raja Ampat and Aru islands, and northeastern Australia (northwestern Torres Strait islands)
Aquila heliaca: breeds central Europe to Mongolia; winters to Africa, northern plains of India, and China
Aquila nipalensis: lowland to montane open habitats, including steppe, grassland, and wooded savanna, from southwestern Russia and Kazakhstan eastward to Mongolia and northeastern China, and southward to Tibetan Plateau; migrates southward to winter in Middle East, Arabian Peninsula, eastern and southern Africa, and southeastern China
Aquila rapax: disjunctly in lowland to montane savanna, open woodland, semi-desert, and arid steppe, of Morocco and Algeria, and in southwestern Arabian Peninsula, and in sub-Saharan Africa (avoiding rainforest), and from southeastern Iran eastward to India and southern Nepal; some post-breeding wandering
Aquila spilogaster: woodland and savanna of sub-Saharan Africa
Aquila verreauxii: locally in sub-Saharan Africa and southern Arabian Peninsula
Ara ambiguus: forest and clearings in lowlands and hills of Caribbean slope, in northeastern Honduras and north-central Nicaragua; southeastern Nicaragua and eastern Costa Rica
Ara ararauna: eastern Panama and Colombia eastward to Venezuela, the Guianas, and northern Brazil, southward to Bolivia and east-central Brazil; formerly occurred in Trinidad (recently reintroduced), Paraguay (where small population persists?, and perhaps northern Argentina
Ara chloropterus: eastern Panama south and east of the Andes, to Bolivia, Brazil, and Paraguay; formerly also northeastern Argentina
Ara macao: humid forest from easternmost Mexico, in Chiapas, northern Guatemala, and Belize, locally eastward in eastern Honduras and northern Nicaragua, southernmost Nicaragua, northern Costa Rica, the Pacific coast of Costa Rica and Panama to the Azuero Peninsula (and including Coiba); in South America in the lowlands of northern Colombia southward along the Magdalena Valley to southern Antioquia; and east of the Andes in the llanos, and Orinoco and Amazon basins from northern Venezuela southward across Amazonia to central Bolivia; in northeastern Brazil eastward to Maranhão
Ara militaris: montane dry to humid and oak-pine forest in Mexico in the Sierra Madre Occidental (central Sonora southward to Oaxaca), and in the Sierra Madre Oriental (eastern Nuevo León and eastern San Luis Potosí), and highly disjunctly in South America in deciduous to humid forest in the foothills of Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, Sierra de Perijá, and the mountains of coastal Venezuela (Falcón eastward to western Anzoategui), and in the western and central Andes of northern Colombia and eastern Andes of south-central Colombia southward in the eastern Andes to the Yungas of northernmost Argentina (Salta)
Ara severus: tropical eastern Panama to the Guianas, northern Bolivia, and Amazonian Brazil
Arachnothera affinis: montane Java and Bali; possibly also montane Sumatra
Arachnothera chrysogenys: southern Myanmar, southern Thailand, Malayan Peninsula, Sumatra, Java, and Borneo
Arachnothera clarae: Luzon, East Visayas, and Mindanao group (northern to southern Philippines)
Arachnothera crassirostris: forest of peninsular Thailand, Malayan Peninsula, Sumatra, and Borneo
Arachnothera everetti: mountains of northern, central, and eastern Borneo
Arachnothera flammifera: East Visayas and Mindanao group (east-central and southern Philippines)
Arachnothera longirostra: lowland to foothill forest understory, secondary forest, coastal scrub, plantations, mangroves, and gardens, patchily in southwestern and eastern India, and from eastern Nepal eastward to south-central China and northern Vietnam, and southward to Greater Sundas and satellite islands, and Bali
Arachnothera magna: Himalayas (from western Nepal) to southern China, western southeastern Asia, Vietnam, and Malayan Peninsula
Arachnothera modesta: tropical rainforest and swamp forest, dry coastal forest, and scrub in the Malayan Peninsula from southernmost Myanmar southward to southern Peninsular Malaysia, Sumatra (including Mentawai Islands), and Borneo
Arachnothera robusta: forest and gardens in the Malayan Peninsula from southernmost Myanmar (southern Tenasserim) and southern Thailand southwards to southern Peninsular Malaysia, Sumatra, Borneo, and Java
Aramides albiventris: Guerrero on Pacific slope and southern Tamaulipas on Caribbean slope of Mexico, southward to Nicaragua and northeastern Costa Rica
Aramides axillaris: coastal northwestern Mexico to Trinidad and Suriname, and to far northwestern Peru
Aramides cajaneus: Costa Rica southward to the Guianas, Brazil, northern Argentina, and Uruguay
Aramides calopterus: eastern Ecuador to northeastern Peru (Loreto) and western Amazonian Brazil
Aramides mangle: coastal eastern Brazil (Maranhão to Rio de Janeiro)
Aramides saracura: forest of southeastern Brazil to Paraguay and northeastern Argentina (Misiones)
Aramides wolfi: western Colombia to southwestern Ecuador and far northern Peru
Aramides ypecaha: marshes of southeastern Brazil to Paraguay, Uruguay, and northeastern Argentina
Aramidopsis plateni: mainly lowland forest and edge, Sulawesi; very local and rare
Aramus guarauna: Florida and increasingly southeastern USA, Greater Antilles, and southern Mexico southward to South America west of the Andes to western Ecuador, and east of the Andes to northern Argentina
Aratinga auricapillus: semi-deciduous forest from eastern Brazil in Alagoas southward along eastern Brazil to Paraná, and to the Cerrado of interior Brazil eastward to Goais, western São Paulo, and easternmost Mato Grosso do Sul
Aratinga jandaya: lowlands of northeastern Brazil (eastern Pará and Goiás to Alagoas)
Aratinga maculata: Brazil (north bank of lower Amazon River in Pará)
Aratinga nenday: Pantanal of southeastern Bolivia, southwestern Brazil, Paraguay, and northern Argentina
Aratinga solstitialis: Guyana, Suriname, and northern Amazonian Brazil
Aratinga weddellii: southeastern Colombia to northern Bolivia and adjacent western Amazonian Brazil
